agency_short: New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS)
admin_note: New Hampshire is a STATE-ADMINISTERED SNAP program — DHHS's Bureau of Family Assistance (BFA) administers directly through District Offices, with no county-level policy variation, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, and New Mexico packs. GENUINE STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: New Hampshire runs THREE parallel eligibility tracks rather than a single BBCE gate — plain "Regular" households (130% FPG gross / 100% FPG net, $3,000 resource limit), "Target" households with an elderly (60+) or disabled member ($4,500 resource limit, still subject to the income tests unless independently categorically eligible), and "Expanded Categorically Eligible" (ECE) households (gross income ≤200% FPG, automatically exempt from any resource test) — see income-and-resources supplement. SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING, a genuine primary-source CONFIRMATION of a minority-position claim several secondary sources repeat with more confidence than a single source alone would justify: New Hampshire fully opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban, effective August 8, 1997, per House Bill 722-FN, Chapter 157, Laws of 1997 (implemented by DHHS SR 97-27) — this pack fetched SR 97-27's own inter-department communication text directly and confirms a felony drug conviction is NOT taken into account for SNAP eligibility in New Hampshire at all, a full opt-out rather than a modified/conditional ban like this roster's Nebraska, Georgia, or several other states carry. THIRD FLAGSHIP FINDING: New Hampshire's Standard Utility Allowance for Heating/Cooling is $1,018/month — a notably high figure this pack cross-checked directly against DHHS's own Table I: SNAP Deductions page — paired with a genuinely distinctive 4-tier utility structure that includes a standalone "Electric-Only" tier ($217) not seen in most other states' 2-or-3-tier utility structures, alongside Utilities-Only ($373) and Telephone-Only ($39); see shelter-utility-deductions supplement. FOURTH FINDING: New Hampshire's STANDARD certification period for non-ESAP households is only 6 months — shorter than the 12-month norm most of this roster's other states use — with a 36-month period reserved for ESAP (all-adult-members elderly/disabled, no earned income) households only; see reporting-certification supplement. Confirm current operative practice with the applicant's own local DHHS District Office, the same caution this roster already carries for its other built states.
system: DHHS's Bureau of Family Assistance (BFA) processes SNAP centrally through District Offices (no county offices with independent policy authority); applicants apply online through NH EASY (nheasy.nh.gov, DHHS's self-service portal), by phone through Client Services (603-271-9700 or 1-800-852-3345 extension 9700, which mails an application), by mail, or in person at a local District Office. The New Hampshire Food Bank operates as a DHHS-partnered SNAP Outreach organization assisting with applications. Households where every adult member is elderly (60+) or disabled with no earned income are certified under the Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP, an FNS demonstration project effective 07/01/2025) for a 36-month certification period with only a yearly reminder to report changes; all other households are certified for 6 months. This pack flags NH's 6-month standard certification period as shorter than most of this roster's other states, see freshness.json.
